newsitem.title: USA: U.S. senator criticizes Swiss over Holocaust plan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. senator criticizes Swiss over Holocaust plan.

text.p: Jewish leaders on Wednesday hailed a Swiss government decision to set up a memorial fund for Holocaust victims but a prominent U.S. senator warned the Swiss they have no business deciding who gets the money.

On a day when Switzerland might have expected praise and a positive reaction, Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato slammed them for their handling of a similar fund in 1962 and said, "The money doesn't belong to them."
"The money was looted from Holocaust victims and should be returned to them. The Swiss must find whose money was looted, how much there is and return it -- all of it," he added.

After months of pressure from the New York Republican and Jewish groups, the Swiss government announced it was setting up a fund with more than $70 million in initial contributions from Swiss banks and other businesses.
It said it would make its own contribution to the fund after a historians' commission made an interim report this spring on Swiss bank collaboration with the Nazis during the Second World War.

The Swiss were accused in U.S. government documents of receiving more than $400 million in looted Nazi gold during the war. Jewish groups also alleged Swiss banks were holding on to millions of dollars in unclaimed assets of Holocaust victims.

Virtually all details of how the fund would work were still to be ironed out, including how it would be administered, who would be in charge and who would qualify for payments, sources close to the negotiations said.

Swiss, Israeli and U.S. diplomats were scheduled to meet on Friday in New York with D'Amato, World Jewish Congress officials and former Federal Reserve Bank chairman Paul Volker, who heads a commission looking into unclaimed assets.
Then on Tuesday, World Jewish Congress Secretary General Israel Singer is to fly to Switzerland for talks with the foreign minister on how the fund would operate.

But D'Amato, reacting to press reports that the Swiss government would administer the fund, was outraged. He said the Swiss botched a similar fund in 1962 when about $10 million in unclaimed assets was discovered in Swiss banks.

The Swiss had asked their banks to turn over unclaimed Second World War accounts but experts said only 26 of 500 banks did so; $8 million went to pay off 944 claimants and the rest went to the Swiss Red Cross and Jewish charities.
D'Amato said the Swiss "failed to adequately notify potential claimants. I am concerned that the Swiss government is trying to follow the same pattern today. We cannot allow business as usual."

His response came just hours after WJC President Edgar Bronfman and other Jewish leaders hailed the Swiss government fund announcement as historic and creating a new chapter in Swiss-Jewish relations.

A WJC spokesman said the senator was right in expressing concern about the 1962 fund and added, "We will continue working with Senator D'Amato. As the U.S. State Department said the other day, he 'is doing the Lord's work.'"
